parties:
Mrs. Tahera Islam ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
The Secretary, Ministry of 'Home affairs, Govt. of Bangladesh and others ------ Opposite parties
full_judgment:
2. The petitioner's case was that her husband Serajul Islam wasa bonafide businessman and Manoaging Director of Shibra Industries Ltd. Sylhet. With a view to set up a Fruit Processing and Canning Industries at an estimated cost of Taka 54 lacs he applied for sanction of loan to Bangladesh Shilpa Bank. The said bank sanctioned Foreign currency equivalent to Taka 10 Iacs and local currency of Taka 14 lacs as loan after compliance of all formalities including mortgage of property and personal guarantee of the Directors of the company. The petitioner's husband after obtaining the loan imported machineries and completed the construction of the project which was due to start in 1982. But due to delay in releasing the proposed loan by the Bank the costs of project increased and the project could not be started in due time. In the mean time the Bank stated Miscellaneous-Case No. 43 of 1985 in the Courtof the District Judge, Sylhet for recovery of the loandues. On 24.2.87 the petitioner's husband was arrested and brought to Dhaka Central Jail and on 25.2.87 a detention order was issued by the Government directing his detention for three months. The grounds of detention were served on 9.3.87. According to the detention order the detention was made in the interest of public safety but according to the grounds served, the detention was made on the ground of non-payment of the loan dues and not  at all on the ground of interest of public safety. Besides that many extraneous grounds were served which were all vague and indefinite. The nonpayment of loan was not a prejudicial act at all and the detention was made illegally and in violation of section 3 of the Special Powers Act because the detention was made not at all to prevent from doing any prejudicial act. Besides that, for the non-payment of the loan specific misc. case as well as criminal case were brought and for that reason also the detention under the Special Powers Act can not be sustained in law. Further there was no order for detention after expiry of the previous extended term which expired on 28.7.87 but still the petitioner's husband was not released and kept under illegal detention and only on 26.8.87 a fresh extension was illegally ordered with retrospective effect. 

 6. Mr. Khonder next submitted that the non-payment of the loan was a mere violation of a civil contract for which appropriate remedy has been provided adequately in P.O. No. 120 of 1972 i.e. Shilpa Bank Order. As a matter of fact the Shilpa Bank has already brought Miscellaneous Case under the provision of Article 33 of the said Order which is pending before the District Judge, Sylhet. So according to Mr. Khondker even if the non-payment of the loan is intentional that can not constitute a prejudicial act with in the meaning of the Special Powers Act. 

 7. On behalf of the State Mr. Syed J.R. Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that in terms of section 2(f)(viii) of the Special Powers Act the intentional non-payment of the loan obtained from the Shilpa Bank constituted a prejudicial act because the economic and financial interest of the State has been prejudiced by the intentional act of the dctenu in non-paying the loan. In this connection the learned Deputy Attorney-General referred to a decision reported in BLD 1986(AD)49 corresponding to 38 DLR(AD)70 in which the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court observed in connection with a similar case of non-payment of loan taken from Shilpa Bank in the following language :- 

 By this reference the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that the non-payment of the dues of the Shilpa Bank prejudicially affects the financial and economic interest of the society and consequently of the State. On the other hand Mr. Wadud Khondker submitted on behalf of the petitioner that the aforesaid observation was on a different context only pointing to the need of early disposal of Shilpa Bank proceeding relating to recovery of loan. In this connection Mr. Khondker also referred to the other parts of the observation of the Appellate Division in the same judgment namely that "the precise remedy for realising its dues is provided in Article 33 of the Order. If any of parties to the proceedings initiated under this Article is aggrieved by an order of the District Judge made thereunder, it may file appeal to the High Court Division of the Supreme Court within 30 days of the date of the order". Mr. Wadud Khondker also referred to the provision of the Shilpa Bank Order and submitted that adequate measures for speedy recovery of the loan were already provided in the said Order and so the Government and the Shilpa Bank could only resort to the said provision as they have already done by starting the Miscellaneous Case and the non-payment of the loan cannot amount to prejudicial act. According to section 2(f)(viii) of the Special Powers Act the prejudicial act means any act which is intended or likely to prejudice the economic and financial interest of the State.' In this case the act of intentional nonpayment of the loan taken from the Shilpa Bank has prejudiced the economic or financial interest of the Shilpa Bank as also the society as has been held in the aforesaid decision and consequently it has prejudiced the economic or financial interest of the State. So the intentional non-payment of the loan can not be said to be outside the ambit of prejudicial act. 

 8. No doubt it is also a civil liability for which remedy has been already sought under Article 33 of the Shilpa Bank Order by starting a Miscellaneous Case which is pending before the District Judge, Sylhet but merely because it is a civil liability it can not be said that there can not be any simultaneous criminal liability. 

 9. Mr. Wadud Khondker by a reference to section 3 of the Special Powers Act submitted that even if non-payment of loan of the Shilpa Bank be a prejudicial act even then the detention can not be ordered in respect of a default which has already been done because section 3 provides for detention only to prevent a person from doing any prejudicial act in future. Section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act as we have already observed provides that the Government may make an order directing-detention only with a view to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. In this case when the detenu had already made default in payment of the loan he had thereby committed prejudicial act already i.e, in the past and there remains no scope for him to do prejudicial act in the same matter in the future. So there is no .scope.to say that the detention was made to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act in future. It is exactly for that reason that in the detention order it was nowhere mentioned that the detention order was considered necessary to prevent the detenue from doing any prejudicial act. Thus it is absolutely clear that the Government had no authority under section 3 of the Special Powers Act or under any other provision of the said Act to order the detention of the petitioner's husband for his having defaulted in repayment of the loan which default had already occurred and prejudicial act if any was also done already with the said default leaving no scope to prevent him from making such default and doing such prejudicial act in future. So we find that the order of detention that was made by the Government directing the detention of the detenu only in the interest of public safety and not at all with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act was illegal and ultravires. In a situation like this namely if the prejudicial act was already done by the dctcnu the Government could have resorted to proceed against them under section 16 of the Special Powers Act. In this connection it was represented on behalf of the petitioner that the detenu was already proceeded against by bringing a criminal case before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate [or the same act of default and on that ground also the petitioner challenged the legality of the detention. It has been held by a Division Bench of this Court reported in 20 DLR 1968 at page 1005 that where specific case has been started in relation to the alleged activity of the detenu the same activity could not in fairness be taken as a reasonable basis for making an order of detention. It has also been similarly held by another Division Bench of this Court in the case of AK.M. Shamsuddin Versus Government of Bangladesh reported in 28 DLR 1976 at page 117 that when two criminal cases were already started on the aforesaid allegations they could not be considered as a ground of detention under the Special Powers Act. So on this ground also the detention is found to be illegal. 

 11. In the result, the rule is made absolute. The detention of the detenu is held to be illegal. Let the detenu Mr. Serajui Islam Chowdhury now detained in jail be set at liberty forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
